assessments.assessment: Source observations: The frontend is a dependency-free collection of standalone HTML routes using native links, one global stylesheet, a shared navigation/toast module, and route-specific JavaScript modules. The Orders route renders and filters a fixed fixture; the Settings route keeps its simulated form and switch state in the DOM; the Customers route contains static customer-card markup while its module imports but does not use the exported customer fixture. No service layer or external data loading path is present in the included source. The supplied smoke tests cover fixture presence and currency formatting, not route interactions. Rendered observations: None; no screenshots or rendered evidence were supplied. Measurements: None; no browser, runtime, build, or performance measurements were performed. Inferences: The fixed, small local fixture and lack of asynchronous loading provide no source evidence of a performance bottleneck, so no performance defect is asserted. Several narrow-screen overflow findings below are inferred from CSS minimum widths and overflow rules and were not rendered. Hypotheses: Actual viewport behavior and dynamic interaction outcomes remain unverified.

assessments.assessment: Source observations: The five routes use ordinary links for navigation. The shared mobile menu opens from its button, closes through the backdrop or Escape, and updates aria-expanded; notifications and supported demo exports show a transient status toast. Orders search and status filtering update the result count and render an empty row when there are no matches. The analytics slider updates its output locally. Customer search hides unmatched cards but does not render an empty state. Settings interactions are local: switches update aria-checked, and the form has a delayed simulated failure path for high thresholds. The included data is described as synthetic and the README describes the fixture as offline. Rendered observations: none; no screenshots are attached and rendered_evidence is empty. Measurements: none taken. Inferences: CSS declares fixed minimum widths for the orders table and settings form row that are likely to cause horizontal overflow at narrow widths; this was not rendered or measured. Hypotheses: the responsive overflow effects need browser confirmation. Network loading and real server recovery behavior are not reachable from the included source, so no claims are made about them.

assessments.assessment: Source observations: The included page templates use link markup for primary navigation. Shared code opens the mobile menu from its button, closes it through the backdrop or Escape, and updates aria-expanded. Notifications and the supported Overview and Analytics exports call a status toast that hides after a timeout. Orders search and status filters update the result count and render an empty row when nothing matches; the View action reveals order details. Customer search hides unmatched cards without rendering an empty state. The Analytics slider updates its output and qualified-order summary locally. Settings switches update aria-checked; Dark mode also shows a confirmation toast but does not apply a workspace theme. A valid settings submission immediately reports success, then changes the live status to a simulated failure when the threshold exceeds $80,000. Several visible customer, orders, and overview controls have no corresponding source-defined interaction. Rendered observations: none; no screenshots are attached. Measurements: none taken. Inferences: the Orders table has a minimum width of 870px while its shell uses overflow:visible, and the Settings contact row has a 720px minimum width that the mobile rule does not reset. Both are likely to cause horizontal overflow at narrow widths, but this was not rendered or measured. The included README describes an offline fixture with synthetic data; real backend loading and recovery behavior cannot be assessed.

assessments.assessment: The overview has a clear, consistent operations-dashboard identity across all three viewports. The desktop layout presents the greeting and actions first, then four KPIs and two side-by-side information panels. Tablet and mobile retain the same palette and typography while progressively stacking content. No visible rendering failure is apparent in the supplied screenshots. The main subjective refinement is that the mobile first viewport is dominated by the KPI stack, leaving the revenue trend and recent activity below the fold.

evidence.description: Desktop view: dark sidebar and white top bar frame a spacious canvas. The greeting and actions lead into four KPI cards, then the revenue chart and recent activity panels.
Tablet view: the top bar uses a menu icon, the KPI cards form a two-column grid, and the chart takes the full content width before the next panel begins.
Mobile view: the greeting and two actions fit above a single-column stack of KPI cards; the fourth card continues past the bottom of the captured viewport.

limitations: The assessment uses only the three supplied screenshots. It does not assess content below the captured viewports or interaction states.
The mobile screenshot shows only the initial viewport, so the report describes the visible KPI emphasis without judging the full-page mobile experience.

assessments.assessment: The supplied screenshots support a consistent, restrained dashboard design: pale cool-gray workspace, white bordered cards, dark blue-gray text, and teal accents. The desktop uses a full-height dark sidebar; tablet and mobile show a compact top bar with a menu icon. At mobile width, the KPI stack dominates the captured content, with only three cards fully visible and part of the fourth; the trend and activity panels are below the captured viewport. The implementation supports the observed reflow: the KPI grid changes from four columns to two below 1180px, the content panels stack at that breakpoint, the sidebar moves off-canvas below 800px, and the KPI grid becomes one column below 520px (assets/styles.css:2, assets/styles.css:7-9; index.html:3, index.html:6-7).

The mobile screenshot shows the compact top bar and a single-column KPI stack; three cards are fully visible and part of the fourth appears at the bottom. The chart and activity panels are outside this captured viewport.
